setup: A 6-month call lets you buy USD 1,000 face of a (then) 6-month zero at USD 990. In 6 months that zero will be worth either USD 987.654 (rate 2.50%) or USD 992.556 (rate 1.50%). Today a 6-month zero costs 0.990099 and a 1-year zero 0.978842 per USD 1 face.
ask: Roughly what is the call worth today, priced by a replicating portfolio?

options.label: ≈ USD 2.6
options.why: That is the down-state payoff, $992.556 - 990$, taken as the value. It ignores that the call pays nothing in the up state and that the payoff is six months away.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.050
options.why: Scale slip: a tenth of the true value.

options.label: ≈ USD 520
options.why: That is the face of 1-year zeros in the replicating portfolio ($F^1 \approx 521$), a position size rather than the call's cost. The short USD 515 of 6-month zeros almost cancels it.

takeaway: The replicating portfolio is two big legs that nearly cancel, so the call is worth a small fraction of its best-case payoff.

setup: You replicate a 6-month call on a zero (payoff USD 0 if the 6-month rate is 2.50%, USD 2.556 if it is 1.50%) using 6-month zeros (face $F^5$) and 1-year zeros (face $F^1$). In 6 months the 6-month zero pays $F^5$ in either state. The 1-year zero is then worth 0.987654 (up) or 0.992556 (down) per USD 1 face.
ask: In the replicating portfolio, is the 6-month-zero position long, short or zero?

options.label: Long
options.why: In the up state the 1-year leg is worth $0.987654\,F^1 > 0$, yet the portfolio must be worth USD 0. Only a short 6-month leg cancels it: $F^5 = -515$.

options.label: Zero
options.why: A 1-year zero on its own is worth a positive amount in both states. It cannot be worth USD 0 in one state and USD 2.556 in the other. A second leg of the opposite sign is required.

takeaway: To replicate a call on a bond, buy the longer zero and short the shorter one. The zero-payoff state forces the short.

setup: A 3-year, 7% annual-coupon bond sits on a recombining rate tree. A European call with strike 100 is exercised on the ex-coupon bond price at year 2, which is USD 98.56, USD 100.62 or USD 102.20 (top, middle, bottom). Year-1 rates are 5.99% (up) and 4.44% (down); today's rate is 3.00%. Risk-neutral up-probabilities are 0.76 today and 0.60 at each year-1 node.
ask: Roughly what is the call worth today?

options.label: ≈ USD 2.2
options.why: That is the best payoff, at the bottom node ($102.20 - 100$). The path there has only $0.24 \times 0.40 \approx 10\%$ probability, and the payoff still has to be discounted.

options.label: ≈ USD 6.3
options.why: The USD 7 coupon was added to the option payoffs, giving $105.56 - 100$ and so on. The coupon goes into the bond's backward induction. Option values carry no coupon.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.045
options.why: Scale slip: a tenth of the true value.

takeaway: An option that pays off only in one corner of the tree is worth a fraction of its best payoff. Coupons go into bond values, never into option values.

setup: A CMT swap on USD 1,000,000 pays $\tfrac{1{,}000{,}000}{2}(y_{CMT} - 7.00\%)$ each half-year. At six months the rate is 7.25% (up) or 6.75% (down), so the payoff there is ±USD 1,250. At one year it is 7.50%, 7.00% or 6.50%, paying +USD 2,500, USD 0 or −USD 2,500. Risk-neutral up-probabilities are 0.76 today and 0.60 at each six-month node. Discount each step at half the node's rate.
ask: Which six-month node value is larger in absolute size, $V_{1,U}$ or $V_{1,L}$?

options.label: $V_{1,L}$
options.why: From the down node, the −USD 2,500 outcome has only 0.40 probability, so its continuation is −USD 967. The up node's continuation is +USD 1,448.

options.label: Equal, since the payoffs are symmetric
options.why: The payoffs are symmetric but the probabilities are 0.60/0.40, which tilts both nodes upward: +USD 2,697.53 against −USD 2,217.35.

takeaway: When the risk-neutral probability is not 0.5, symmetric payoffs do not produce symmetric node values.

setup: A CMT swap on USD 1,000,000 pays $\tfrac{1{,}000{,}000}{2}(y_{CMT} - 7.00\%)$ each half-year. At six months the rate is 7.25% (up) or 6.75% (down), so the payoff there is ±USD 1,250. At one year it is 7.50%, 7.00% or 6.50%, paying +USD 2,500, USD 0 or −USD 2,500. Today's rate is 7.00%. Risk-neutral up-probabilities are 0.76 today and 0.60 at each six-month node. Discount each step at half the node's rate.
ask: Roughly what is the swap worth today to the CMT receiver?

options.label: ≈ USD 150,000
options.why: Rates entered as percent numbers: $7.25 - 7.00 = 0.25$ used in place of $0.0025$. Every payoff is 100× too large.

options.label: ≈ USD 15m
options.why: Rate gaps entered in basis points: 25 used in place of 0.0025. Every payoff is 10,000× too large.

options.label: ≈ USD 150
options.why: Scale slip: a tenth of the true value.

takeaway: A 25 bp rate gap on half of USD 1m is USD 1,250 per period. Size one payoff first, and the swap's value follows in the low thousands.

setup: A risk-neutral tree prices a CMT swap at USD 1,466.63. The swap trades in the market at USD 1,464.40. You solve for the option-adjusted spread: one constant spread added to every discount rate in the tree so that the model value equals the market price.
ask: Is the OAS positive, negative or zero?

options.label: Negative
options.why: A negative spread lowers the discount rates and raises the model value, which pushes it further above the market price.

options.label: Zero
options.why: A zero OAS would mean the model already matches the market. The USD 2.23 gap needs a spread, about +20 bp here.

working.label: Market minus model
working.display: $1{,}464.40 - 1{,}466.63 = -2.23$: the market is below the model

working.label: Fix
working.display: Lower the model value by raising every discount rate

takeaway: Market price below model price → raise the discount rates → positive OAS.

setup: A trader sells USD 100m face of a T-bond (DV01 0.068 per USD 100 face) and hedges it by buying TIPS (DV01 0.084 per USD 100 face). The hedge is DV01-neutral: both yields are assumed to move by the same number of basis points.
ask: Is the TIPS face amount more than, less than or equal to USD 100m?

options.label: More than USD 100m
options.why: This inverts the ratio: $100 \times 0.084/0.068 = \text{USD }123.5$m. The TIPS is the more rate-sensitive bond, so less face is needed.

options.label: Equal to USD 100m
options.why: Equal face amounts hedge only if the DV01s are equal. They are 0.068 and 0.084.

takeaway: In a DV01 hedge, a more sensitive hedging instrument means a smaller face amount.

setup: The DV01-neutral hedge for a USD 100m T-bond short is USD 80.95m of TIPS. A regression of nominal yield changes on real yield changes, $\Delta y^N = \alpha + \beta\,\Delta y^R + \epsilon$, gives $\beta = 1.0198$.
ask: Moving to the regression hedge, does the TIPS face go up, go down or stay the same?

options.label: Goes down
options.why: That divides by $\beta$. Nominal yields move 1.0198 bp per 1 bp of real yield, so each TIPS basis point has to offset slightly more T-bond P&L. Multiply by $\beta$.

options.label: Stays the same
options.why: That holds only if $\beta = 1$. With $\beta = 1.0198$ the DV01 hedge is scaled up: $80.95 \times 1.0198 = \text{USD }82.55$m.

takeaway: When $\beta > 1$ (nominal yields move more than real yields), buy more of the real bond than the DV01-neutral amount.

setup: A trader who receives fixed on an illiquid 20-year euro swap hedges with 10-year and 30-year swaps. The regression $\Delta y^{20} = \alpha + \beta^{10}\Delta y^{10} + \beta^{30}\Delta y^{30} + \epsilon$ gives $\beta^{10} = 0.2221$ and $\beta^{30} = 0.7765$ ($R^2 = 99.8\%$).
ask: Before computing face values: which hedge leg carries more of the 20-year swap's DV01?

options.label: The 10-year leg
options.why: The 10-year risk weight is 0.2221, which covers only about 22% of the 20-year DV01.

options.label: About 50/50, since 20 is midway between 10 and 30
options.why: That is maturity interpolation. The regression shows the 20-year rate moving mostly with the 30-year: 77.65% against 22.21%.

working.label: Face values next
working.display: $F^{10} = -\dfrac{F^{20} DV01^{20}}{DV01^{10}}\beta^{10}$, and likewise for $F^{30}$, each divided by its own DV01

takeaway: In a two-variable regression hedge the betas are DV01 shares. Read them before thinking about face amounts.

setup: To hedge a corporate bond with a Treasury, regressing corporate yield changes on Treasury yield changes gives $\beta = 0.842$ (risk weight 84.2%). The reverse regression, Treasury changes on corporate changes, gives $\beta = 0.921$.
ask: Is the reverse regression's implied risk weight above or below 100%?

options.label: Below 100%
options.why: 0.921 is the reverse regression's slope. The implied risk weight is its reciprocal: $1/0.921 = 108.6\%$.

options.label: The same 84.2%
options.why: Least squares is not symmetric. The two regressions agree only when the fit is perfect, and here the reverse regression implies 108.6%.

takeaway: For a reverse regression, invert the slope to get the risk weight, and expect a different answer from the direct regression.

setup: A USD 950m bond portfolio defaults with probability 2%, and a default loses 40% of principal. Otherwise there is no loss.
ask: Before computing expected shortfall: what is the 95% VaR?

options.label: USD 380m
options.why: Default occupies only the worst 2% of outcomes, so the 95th-percentile outcome is no default. USD 380m is the loss given default.

options.label: USD 7.6m
options.why: That is the expected loss, $0.02 \times 380$. VaR is a quantile, not a mean, and at the 95th percentile the loss is zero.

working.label: 95% VaR
working.display: $\text{PD} = 2\% < 5\%$, so the 95th-percentile outcome is no default: VaR $= \text{USD }0$

takeaway: When the loss event is rarer than the tail probability, VaR reports zero. That is the blind spot FRTB fixes by moving to ES.

setup: A USD 950m bond portfolio defaults with probability 2%, and a default loses 40% of principal. Otherwise there is no loss. Take the 95% expected shortfall as the average loss across the worst 5% of outcomes.
ask: Roughly how large is the 95% expected shortfall?

options.label: ≈ USD 380m
options.why: That is the loss given default. The worst 5% of outcomes is 2% default (loss USD 380m) and 3% no loss, so the tail average is $0.4 \times 380$.

options.label: ≈ USD 950m
options.why: This takes the whole principal, ignoring the 40% loss severity and the averaging across the tail.

options.label: ≈ USD 7.6m
options.why: That is the expected loss over all outcomes, $0.02 \times 380$, not the average across the tail.

working.label: 95% VaR
working.display: Default is only 2% of outcomes, so VaR $= 0$

takeaway: ES averages over the whole tail: a 2% loss event inside a 5% tail gets a weight of 2/5.

setup: A desk's daily losses are normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. Its capital measure changes from the 99% VaR, $\mu + 2.326\sigma$, to the FRTB 97.5% expected shortfall.
ask: For this normal portfolio, what happens to the risk number?

options.label: Rises sharply, because ES averages the tail
options.why: A normal tail is thin, so the average beyond the 97.5% cut lands only 0.012$\sigma$ past the 99% VaR. The two measures separate sharply only when tails are fat.

options.label: Falls, because 97.5% is a lower confidence level
options.why: A lower cut on its own would reduce the number. ES then averages beyond that cut, which almost exactly offsets it: $2.338\sigma$ against $2.326\sigma$.

takeaway: For normal returns, 97.5% ES ≈ 99% VaR. The switch matters only when the tails are fat.

setup: At the start of Year 1, King Bank has assets of USD 125m earning 6.00%, liabilities of USD 75m paying 5.00%, and equity of USD 50m. At the end of Year 1, USD 25m of assets expire. No liabilities expire in Year 1.
ask: Roughly what is the term structure of expected cumulated cash flows (TSECCF) at the end of Year 1?

options.label: ≈ USD 3.8m
options.why: Interest only, $7.50 - 3.75$. The expiring USD 25m asset is itself a positive cash flow.

options.label: ≈ USD 130m
options.why: This counts the whole USD 125m asset book as cash coming in. Only the USD 25m that expires produces a principal flow.

options.label: ≈ USD 400m
options.why: Rates entered as whole numbers: $6 \times 125 - 5 \times 75 = 375$, plus 25.

takeaway: Year-1 TSECCF = expiring assets + interest earned − interest paid − any expiring liabilities.

setup: King Bank's TSECCF at the end of Year 1 is +USD 28.75m. In Year 2 its remaining USD 100m of assets earn 6.00%. Liabilities of USD 75m pay 5.00% for the full year, and USD 15m of them expire at the end of Year 2.
ask: Is TSECCF at the end of Year 2 positive, negative or too close to call?

options.label: Negative
options.why: Year 2's own net flow is $6.00 - 15 - 3.75 = -\text{USD }12.75$m. That is the TSECF entry for the year. The cumulative figure also carries forward the +USD 28.75m.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: $28.75 - 12.75 = +16.00$ leaves a wide margin.

takeaway: TSECCF is cumulative, so a negative year does not make it negative as long as earlier years built a cushion.

setup: A bank enters a sell/buyback. At the start it sells a bond and receives USD 307,200, which is recorded in its cumulated liquidity generation capacity. At the end it buys the bond back for USD 307,350.
ask: At the end date, which way does the bank's TSECF move?

options.label: Up
options.why: The USD 307,200 received at the start went to TSCLGC, not TSECF. At the end the bank pays USD 150 more than it received, which is a net outflow.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The two legs do not wash out. The USD 150 difference, the funding interest, enters TSECF on the end date.

takeaway: In a sell/buyback, LGC rises at the start and TSECF falls by the interest at the end.

setup: A bank enters a buy/sellback. At the start it pays USD 500,000 for 40,000 bonds. At the end it sells them back and receives USD 501,000, including accrued interest.
ask: At the start, what happens to the bank's cumulated liquidity generation capacity (TSCLGC)?

options.label: Rises by USD 500,000
options.why: That is the sell/buyback pattern. In a buy/sellback cash goes out and no liquidity is generated. The bonds are added to TSAA instead.

options.label: Falls by USD 500,000
options.why: The USD 500,000 outflow is recorded in TSECF, not TSCLGC. LGC is not modified at either end.

takeaway: A sell/buyback generates LGC at the start. A buy/sellback never does.

setup: A corporate customer draws on its committed credit line at a fixed contract rate that is now below the current market rate. The bank has to fund the drawdown at market rates.
ask: What is the financial impact of this exercise on the bank?

options.label: Positive
options.why: That is the customer's view: borrowing below market is good for the customer. The bank lends below its own market funding cost.

options.label: Zero, since it is only a cash-flow event
options.why: Exercise changes the balance sheet (cash goes out) and also has a financial impact, set by the contract rate against market conditions.

working.label: Customer
working.display: Borrows below market: a gain for the customer

working.label: Bank
working.display: Earns the contract rate, pays the market rate: a loss for the bank

takeaway: Sign a liquidity option's impact from the bank's side. It is the opposite of the customer's.

setup: A bank expects an inflow of USD 100m on a date. At the 95% confidence level, the actual inflow could be as low as USD 90m.
ask: Is the positive cash flow at risk ($\text{cfaR}^{+}$), as reported, positive, negative or zero?

options.label: Negative (−USD 10m)
options.why: Actual minus expected, $90 - 100$, gives $-10$. $\text{cfaR}^{+}$ is expected minus actual, and it is reported as a positive shortfall.

options.label: Zero
options.why: The inflow does fall short, by USD 10m. Zero would mean no adverse surprise.

takeaway: cfaR is always reported as a positive adverse surprise: expected − actual for inflows, actual − expected for outflows.

setup: Under a CSA with a threshold of 100, no initial margin and no MTA, the portfolio was worth 250 at Time 1 and 150 of collateral was called, which is now held. At Time 2 the portfolio is worth 225.
ask: At Time 2, is the credit support amount positive (call more), negative (return collateral) or zero?

options.label: Positive: call more
options.why: It is true that $225 - 150 = 75$ is uncollateralized, but the first 100 is the threshold and is never collateralized. Required collateral is $225 - 100 = 125$, and 150 is held.

options.label: Zero
options.why: Required collateral is 125 and 150 is held, so 25 is surplus and has to be returned.

takeaway: Uncollateralized exposure can still be positive while the credit support amount is negative. The threshold slice is never covered.

setup: Under a CSA with a threshold of 100, no initial margin and no MTA, the portfolio was worth 250 at Time 1 and 150 of collateral was called, which is now held. At Time 2 the portfolio is worth 225.
ask: Before any collateral moves at Time 2, roughly how much of the exposure is uncollateralized?

options.why: That is the size of the credit support amount ($-25$, a return of collateral), not the uncollateralized exposure.
This ignores the 150 of collateral already held.
Scale slip: a tenth of the true value.

takeaway: Uncollateralized exposure (value minus collateral held) and the credit support amount are different numbers. Keep them apart.

setup: Collateral held against a counterparty is $\max(\text{value} - K_c, 0) + \mathrm{IM}_c$. The portfolio is worth 250. The CSA changes from threshold $K_c = 100$ with no initial margin to threshold $K_c = 0$ with initial margin of 40.
ask: What happens to the total collateral the bank holds?

options.label: Falls
options.why: Both changes add collateral. Removing the threshold collateralizes the first 100, and the initial margin is posted on top.

options.label: Roughly unchanged
options.why: Threshold and initial margin only offset when one rises as the other is added. Here both changes add collateral: dropping the threshold adds 100 and the initial margin adds 40, so 150 becomes 290.

takeaway: Threshold and initial margin pull in opposite directions: a higher threshold means less collateral, and more initial margin means more.
